subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Price Volatility and Farmers
description: A fast breakdown of Price Volatility and Farmers for builders.

hook.text: Coffee prices can swing 30% in a single year. Farmers plant trees that take 3–5 years to fruit.

buildup.text: By the time new trees produce, the market may have crashed. Farmers can't pivot like a factory can.

discovery.text: Futures contracts let roasters lock in prices months ahead. But most small farmers can't access these markets.

twist.text: When prices spike, farmers benefit briefly—but quickly face higher input costs as fertilizer and labor rise too.

climax.text: Volatility is the constant enemy. It makes it impossible to plan, invest, or escape the poverty cycle.

punchline.text: You can't plan a life around prices that change every day.

quiz.question: Why can't small coffee farmers hedge against price swings?
options: Most lack access to futures markets and financial tools

details.summary: Coffee prices can swing 30 to 50 percent within a single year. Farmers plant trees that take years to produce, making it impossible to adjust supply quickly. This mismatch between long agricultural cycles and short-term market swings traps producers in perpetual financial uncertainty.
details.whyItMatters: Price volatility is the root cause of poverty in coffee farming. Without mechanisms to stabilize income, farmers cannot invest in quality or their own futures.
takeaways: Coffee prices can fluctuate 30 to 50 percent in a year
Trees take 3 to 5 years to produce, limiting supply responses
Volatility prevents farmers from long-term planning

faq.question: What causes coffee price crashes?
faq.answer: Overproduction is the most common trigger, often following a period of high prices that encouraged planting. Brazil's massive harvests can flood the market. Currency devaluation in producing countries also makes their coffee cheaper on world markets, dragging prices down.

faq.question: How can farmers protect themselves from price swings?
faq.answer: Options include joining cooperatives for collective bargaining, diversifying crops, pursuing fair trade or direct trade relationships, and using futures contracts. However, most smallholders lack access to financial tools that larger agribusinesses use to hedge.
